name: OPC UA
verifiedAgainst: Ignition, secured and signed in
Independent OPC UA servers in two languages
Bare metal (2026-11-17)
summary: Prefer this one when a device offers a choice. It browses, it is properly secured, and it subscribes.
trap: A node's position number depends on the order the server loaded things. Add a namespace or upgrade firmware and position 3 quietly becomes something else, so every reading is wrong with no error anywhere. HotLoop addresses by name so that can't happen to you.
body: The driver subscribes rather than polls. The server sends a value when it changes, at a rate it can sustain, instead of being asked the same question every scan by a client with no idea whether anything moved. If a server refuses a subscription, the driver falls back to batched reads rather than failing the device.

Addresses use the stable name of a node, not its position, so a server reload or a firmware upgrade never quietly points a tag at the wrong thing. A typo is caught when you save it, not three weeks later when a tag reads bad forever.

name: Modbus TCP/RTU
verifiedAgainst: Real Modbus servers over TCP
Bare metal (2026-11-17)
summary: The 1979 workhorse. PLCs, VFDs, power meters, RTUs, and the fallback of every gateway that has nothing better.
trap: Word order is the setting people get wrong, and a float read with the wrong order is not obviously wrong on a screen. It is a plausible number that is not the truth.
body: All four word orders are supported, under the names vendor manuals print: ABCD, CDAB, BADC, and DCBA. Set a device default and override it per tag.

Addressing follows your drawings: if they use the traditional 40001-style numbering, one setting lets you write the numbers straight from them. Getting this wrong by one is the oldest Modbus bug there is.
Reads are merged into blocks, so neighboring registers become one request and a busy serial line gets some peace.
Writing a single bit of a holding register keeps the other fifteen bits intact, because Modbus has no atomic bit-set there.

name: MQTT and Sparkplug B
verifiedAgainst: Eclipse Mosquitto, with crafted Sparkplug frames
Bare metal (2026-11-17)
summary: Plain MQTT, or Sparkplug B as a full primary host application.
trap: Delivering Sparkplug messages concurrently reorders them, which makes a healthy node look like it is dropping messages and provokes a storm of re-announcements. HotLoop keeps message order.
body: As a Sparkplug B primary host, the driver does the things the specification asks for and most integrations skip.

Edge nodes can see the host drop instead of guessing from a timeout. The host tracks every node's sequence, asks a node to re-announce itself when it skips or after the host's own reconnect, and matches a death to the right birth, so a stale death certificate from a previous session can't kill the current one.

name: EtherNet/IP
verifiedAgainst: Address, batching, and type-mapping tests on CIP frames
Run on a bare-metal host (2026-11-17)
summary: Allen-Bradley ControlLogix, CompactLogix, and Micro820. Tags have names, so the controller can be asked what it holds.
trap: The controller rejects a read whose declared type does not match, so the type has to come from somewhere. Unknown falls back to a REAL, which most process values are.
body: The data type comes from the tag, or from an explicit suffix, which wins.
Reads are batched, falling back to single reads when a batch fails, so one bad tag path does not blind the other nineteen.
notVerifiedNote: Check a value you already know on the controller at commissioning before trusting a screen.

name: S7comm
verifiedAgainst: Frame-level decode and encode tests
Run on a bare-metal host (2026-11-17)
summary: Siemens S7-300, S7-400, S7-1200, and S7-1500, over ISO-on-TCP by rack and slot.
trap: The type is required for anything wider than a byte. The protocol cannot tell you whether four bytes are a REAL or a DINT, because that is a fact about the PLC program, not about the wire.
body: Defaults suit an S7-1200 or S7-1500, and an S7-300 or S7-400 usually needs one setting changed.
HotLoop uses the plain connection type, so it does not occupy the connection an engineer wants for TIA Portal.
There is no browse: a CPU does not publish the layout of its data blocks, because that lives in the TIA Portal project.
notVerifiedNote: Check a value you already know on the PLC at commissioning before trusting a screen. Set the type of anything wider than a byte from the PLC program.

name: MTConnect
verifiedAgainst: Golden MTConnect agent documents, served by a test HTTP server
summary: Read-only machine tool telemetry. MTConnect has no command channel, so this driver reads only.
trap: UNAVAILABLE is the agent explicitly saying it has no reading. It becomes bad quality, not the text "UNAVAILABLE" and not zero.
body: Two details separate a working integration from a plausible one. First, UNAVAILABLE becomes bad quality rather than a string or a zero. Second, a Condition's meaning is its state (Normal, Warning, Fault, or Unavailable), not its text, which is usually empty.
Browse walks the machine's whole component tree to any depth, so you pick data points instead of typing paths.
notVerifiedNote: Compare a value on the machine's own display with what HotLoop reads, at commissioning.

name: HTTP and REST
verifiedAgainst: Recorded JSON documents, served by a test HTTP server
summary: The catch-all, for energy meters, environmental sensors, OEM controllers, and the REST side of a gateway that speaks something proprietary underneath.
trap: These APIs love returning an unordered array of name and value objects, and indexing by position is a bug waiting for a firmware update. Select by field value instead.
body: One request serves every tag on the device. Browse walks the document and reports every value with the path that reaches it.
notVerifiedNote: Compare one value from the device's API with the device's own reading, at commissioning.

name: UniFi Network
verifiedAgainst: Real UniFi consoles, logged in as a view-only account
Real UniFi switches and a backup WAN
summary: The plant network as a device: switches, ports, PoE, WAN failover and clients as tags, plus commands you arm to restart, power-cycle or block.
trap: A WAN block can say up with a stale signal while the backup link has been unplugged for days. The driver reads the console's own health checks instead, so a dead backup reads down.
body: One login per console, reused for every read, and never more than one read every ten seconds whatever the poll interval says. Make a local account on the console, because a Ubiquiti cloud account can't sign in from a script. View-only is enough to read, and commands need a local Administrator.
The console's certificate is pinned. You confirm its identity once, and a console with a different key is refused before the password goes anywhere.

Switches, ports, PoE draw, WAN links, clients, and the site's health come in as tags that create themselves as gear is adopted, and go bad quality instead of vanishing. A switch dropping off is in the logbook when it happens.

It reads the whole network and it acts on it. Restart a device, power-cycle a PoE port, set a port's PoE mode, or block a client and let it back in. Each command is created read-only and is sent only after a person arms it through the write gate. A port is power-cycled at most once in 15 minutes, and an uplink port is never cycled. The screens, the topology map and the events are on the UniFi page.

name: SNMP
verifiedAgainst: A standard SNMP agent, read over v1, v2c, and v3 at every security level, on UDP and TCP
Bare metal (2026-11-17)
summary: Switches, UPSs, PDUs, power meters, and any Linux box running snmpd, read-only. HotLoop never sends a SET.
trap: A wrong community answers with nothing. An SNMPv1 or v2c agent drops a request carrying a community it does not know, so a wrong community, a wrong port, a firewall, and an agent that is down all look like a timeout. HotLoop's message names all four. SNMPv3 does tell them apart.
body: Read-only, always. HotLoop never sends an SNMP SET, because a SET can change a switch's configuration, and the point of this driver is to see the plant network, not to run it.
There is no default community, because "public" is how a plant's switches get read by whoever asks. The community and the v3 passphrases are stored encrypted like every other device secret.
Counters report what the agent sent, and uptime is scaled to seconds for you. An object the agent does not have is a bad reading with the reason, and the others in the same request still read.
Point HotLoop at a device and it asks what it needs, looks at the real device, and keeps the points you choose, with nothing armed.

name: BACnet/IP
verifiedAgainst: An independent BACnet stack serving every object type HotLoop reads
Frames recorded off that device
Bare metal (2026-11-17)
notVerifiedHeading: Tested against an independent BACnet stack, and on bare metal.
notVerifiedNote: A controller on an MS/TP trunk behind a BACnet router can't be reached directly. Address the router's own BACnet/IP side, or put a gateway in front. Vendors differ about their object lists and how they answer a request that is too big, so a new controller is still a commissioning job.
summary: Building controllers, meters, and thermostats on the IP network, read-only. HotLoop never writes a BACnet property.
trap: Status flags are part of the reading. An object whose fault flag is set reads bad, with the reason. One that is out of service or overridden reads uncertain, because its present value is something a person or a program put there, not a measurement.
body: Read-only, on purpose. A BACnet write lands on a commandable output through a priority array, and a priority left set holds the equipment where it was put after whoever set it has gone home. That is a feature to design deliberately, not one to leave lying around.
Connecting asks the device who it is. Set the device instance and a different device answering at a reused address, or a swapped controller, is refused instead of read.
A device whose answer will not fit one frame is asked for fewer objects at a time, and an object that is not there fails its own tag and no other.
Point HotLoop at a device and nothing it makes is armed.

name: CODESYS
verifiedAgainst: A real CODESYS Control for Linux runtime running a lab program, plus a program of over a hundred thousand variables read in about two seconds, reads and writes
Bare metal (2026-11-17)
notVerifiedHeading: Tested against a real runtime, and on bare metal.
summary: A CODESYS PLC, read and written by the names its programmer gave the variables, through the runtime's own OPC UA server.
trap: A PLC with no Symbol Configuration publishes nothing a client can read. The program has to export the variables you want, and a variable is writable from HotLoop only when its symbol is read and write. HotLoop's setup message says to add one.
body: CODESYS documents one way for a third party to read a controller's variables, and it is the runtime's own OPC UA server, so that is what this driver uses. Nothing is installed in your PLC project beyond the Symbol Configuration.
Discovery lists what the application exports, with the types and the access the programmer gave them, and walks into arrays and structures.

A restart or a download drops the session. Every tag reads bad with the reason, and HotLoop reconnects by itself and reads the symbols as they are now. Requests are shaped to the limits the runtime publishes.

name: OPC UA PubSub (UADP)
verifiedAgainst: An independent OPC UA stack, in both directions over multicast, in both encodings and with key and delta frames
HotLoop Transmitter, publishing from inside a CODESYS PLC
notVerifiedHeading: Tested in both directions against an independent stack, and against a CODESYS PLC.
notVerifiedNote: Message security, chunking, discovery, events and structure fields are not supported. A datagram that uses one is refused by name, counted by reason, and never guessed at.
summary: A publisher sends DataSets as UDP datagrams to whoever listens, unicast or multicast. HotLoop subscribes as a device and publishes as a setting.
trap: A machine with more than one network card has to say which one joins the multicast group, or the join fails. Name the interface on the device.
body: A lost message, a gap in the sequence numbers, marks that writer's tags uncertain until its next full update, because a change may have gone with it. A writer that goes silent reads bad, and a field the publisher marks bad or uncertain is that.
Edge and the Gateway can also publish the tags you choose as OPC UA PubSub, switched off until you switch it on. A bad tag goes out as its status, never as its last value.
The subscriber is read-only. HotLoop Transmitter is the publisher that runs inside a CODESYS PLC, and this is the driver that listens to it.

name: Everything else
summary: Eight protocols with no driver, by choice, reached through the gateway a site already has.
body: PROFINET, EtherCAT, HART, DNP3, FINS, MELSEC/SLMP, CANopen, and FANUC FOCAS are not spoken natively, and there is no driver for them. That is a deliberate choice, not a gap waiting to be filled with a stub.

Sites running these protocols almost always already have a gateway that re-publishes on OPC UA or Modbus, such as a PROFINET IO controller with an OPC UA server, or a HART multiplexer with a Modbus map. Point a device at that endpoint and configure it as OPC UA or Modbus.

Eight more drivers that each duplicate what a site's existing gateway already does would be eight more things to get subtly wrong, on the equipment that is hardest to test against. If a site genuinely has no gateway and needs one of these natively, that is a real piece of work to schedule.
There are no placeholder drivers. A protocol either has a working implementation or it is on this page.
